> Intro

>     See [[slug]] here

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool carries at least four
columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four more on top of whatever its children
already had — so a marker glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is
the defect, not a style question.

> - A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has to wrap at least once at
>   every width under test so that its continuation lines are visible next to its own
>   marker rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
> - A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a continuation line, so that the
>   alignment of the two items against each other can be compared directly at a width
>   where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are never substituted for a
glyph, so the library still spells them as digits when the last pass over the body runs:

> 1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its
>    continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.
> 2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list under it so that the drift the
>    re-alignment pass subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside one.
>    - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap at the widths under test, so its
>      own continuation column is observable.
>    - A second nested item, kept short.
> 3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted prose under it does, and
is reflowed through the same seam:

> ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one line
>
> The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the two are checked against
> the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom of it — two indents
still pending when the innermost list composes its body:

> > - The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum
> >   of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
> > - A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote **inside** a list item is *legitimately* indented past
its item's text column by its own renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

- A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own before it that is long enough
  to wrap at the widths under test:

  > Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at every width under test, and
  > deliberately indented deeper than the item's own text column by the blockquote
  > renderer rather than by any defect.

  Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough to wrap, which must land
  back at the item's own text column rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows, exactly as fenced code
does everywhere else in this tool, and stays inside a recorded code range:

> A quote that introduces a command.
>
> ```bash
> some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
> ```
>
> Trailing prose after the fence.

A **one-line** fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that decides how strict the
sentinel walk has to be, because its whole content sits on a line that both opens and
closes the sentinel pair:

> ```
> one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim
> ```

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both passes that walk a composed
body meet a sentinel in the same document:

> - An item introducing a command:
>
>   ```sh
>   another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
>   ```
>
> - A second item, long enough to wrap so that the item after a fence is still measured.

Plain quoted prose with no list in it at all, as the control: it is reflowed by the
library at the blockquote's own budget, so none of its lines should need the safety net,
and none of them should start at column 0.

> A plain blockquoted paragraph with no list in it, long enough to wrap at every width
> under test, included because the same indent that the list case loses is the one this
> case loses too — the mechanism is the blockquote's, not the list's.

        1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.

            • The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.

# Coalesced-path guard collision

The committed witness for WP-1 of `plans/renderer-deferred-work.md`. Every list below is
**tight** and every item's source spans two authored lines, so the renderer's coalescing
seam joins them and re-wraps them itself rather than leaving the wrap to the
post-composition pass. Each item carries a bare `*` in its prose, positioned so that at
some width the re-wrap starts a continuation line with it.

The one-digit ordered marker is the defect case: the item's text column is 7, and one
guard space put it at 8, exactly on the four-column grid, where the bullet substitution
claimed the line. Width 65 corrupted; 64 and 66 were clean.

short of the grid — so the same collision reappears at a different width (69).

  and continues on a second authored source line * star token here and more words to push it over

The unordered marker's text column is 6, so one guard space lands at 7 and misses the grid:

# Fenced code inside list items

The WP-2f fixture. Two invariants live here, both invisible to every width gate:
`rewrapListBody` must never rewrite a line that belongs to a fenced block, and it must
never choose a line break that leaves a continuation line starting `*` or `N.`.

- A loose item whose fence carries a command far longer than any target width under
  test, which this pass used to split mid-command:

  ```bash
  echo "a deliberately very long command line that must never be rewrapped or reindented at all, at any width"
  ```

- A loose item with a **one-line** fence — the case that decides how strict the sentinel
  walk has to be, because the block's opening and closing markers land on the same
  physical line and so that line never *starts* inside a fence:

  ```bash
  printf '%s\n' "one physical line, opening and closing marker both on it, and still far too long to fit"
  ```

- A tight item with a fence, whose content carries both marker shapes as decoys:
  ```text
  * not a bullet, and 1. not a marker, on a line long enough that the pass would have split it
  ```

- An outer item, long enough to wrap on its own, so that the level below it is not the
  only thing this pass has to look at.

  - A nested item whose fence has to survive the shallower level's pass as well as its
    own, since every level runs this pass over the body it just composed:

    ```bash
    git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all --since="2026-01-01" --author="nobody" | head -40
    ```

- A second outer item.

An ordered list, so the renumbering pass runs over a body that contains a fence:

1. An ordered item carrying a fence of its own:

   ```bash
   rsync -avz --delete --exclude='*.tmp' ./source/ user@host.example.invalid:/srv/destination/
   ```

2. A second ordered item, which must keep its own number.

The marker-shaped-continuation case, which needs no fence at all — the pass chooses
where this item breaks, and one of the breaks lands on a bare `*`:

1. An ordered item padding word here to move the break point along by a measured amount and then * zero or more, not a bullet, and the item continues for a while after it so the line is long.
2. A second item that must keep its own number.
3. A third item that must keep its own number.

# Loose list probe A loose list is any list where at least one item ends with a blank line. The lexer stamps looseness onto the whole list, so every item below routes through mdview's own paragraph override even though only the separation between them is blank. ## Loose list — the defect case - This first item is deliberately long enough that it must wrap across several rendered lines at any reasonable terminal width, so that the double-reflow defect has room to show itself clearly in the output stream. - The second item exists purely so that the list contains a blank line between items, which is what makes marked stamp the entire list as loose and route every item through mdview's own paragraph override, a live seam. - A third long item, again written at sufficient length that the wrapping engine has to break it multiple times, which is precisely the condition under which the orphaned trailing word appears at the end of each wrapped segment. ## Loose list with a nested loose list - An outer item carrying enough text to wrap at every width under test, so that the outer nesting level exercises the same wrapping budget the flat case does before recursion is considered at all. - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap, which matters because the nested level is wrapped against a strictly smaller budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower pass that runs afterwards. - A second nested item, present so the inner list also ends an item on a blank line and is therefore stamped loose in its own right rather than inheriting the outer list's state. - A closing outer item, long enough to wrap, confirming that the outer list resumes at the outer budget once the nested list has been rendered and folded back into the parent body. ## Loose list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive - A hard break follows this sentence.
And this sentence must begin a new rendered line of its own, even though the line before it is far too short to have been broken by any wrapping engine, and even though this item is long enough to wrap several times afterwards. - A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test so that the item is not trivially short. ## Loose ordered list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide 1. The first ordered loose item, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, so a budget computed from a hardcoded two-column marker would shear the tail of every line it produces. 2. Second. 3. Third. 4. Fourth. 5. Fifth. 6. Sixth. 7. Seventh. 8. Eighth. 9. Ninth. 10. The tenth ordered loose item, also long enough to wrap at every width under test — this is the item whose marker is four columns wide rather than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong. ## Tight list — the control, must not change - A tight list item written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, which is the point: tight items never reach the paragraph override at all, so this rendering is the reference the loose case should match. - A second tight item, also long enough to wrap across multiple lines, with no blank line separating it from its neighbour so the lexer leaves the whole list tight. - A third tight item, again long, closing the control list without introducing any blank line that would flip the list into the loose branch being fixed. ## Ordered tight list — a second control 1. An ordered tight item long enough to wrap, verifying that the ordered marker path is unaffected by whatever the loose-list fix does to the unordered one. 2. A second ordered item, also long enough to wrap over several lines at the widths under test. ## Plain prose — the non-list control This paragraph is not part of any list and is deliberately long enough to be reflowed by the paragraph renderer at every width under test, so that any change to non-list prose wrapping shows up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather than hiding in a corpus. > A blockquote, also long enough to wrap at every width under test, included because the blockquote renderer reads the same reflow flag the paragraph renderer does and must therefore be held as a control alongside it.

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool carries at least four
columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four more on top of whatever its children
already had — so a marker glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is
the defect, not a style question.

> - A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has to wrap at least once at
>   every width under test so that its continuation lines are visible next to its own
>   marker rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
> - A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a continuation line, so that the
>   alignment of the two items against each other can be compared directly at a width
>   where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are never substituted for a
glyph, so the library still spells them as digits when the last pass over the body runs:

> 1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its
>    continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.
> 2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list under it so that the drift the
>    re-alignment pass subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside one.
>    - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap at the widths under test, so its
>      own continuation column is observable.
>    - A second nested item, kept short.
> 3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted prose under it does, and
is reflowed through the same seam:

> ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one line
>
> The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the two are checked against
> the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom of it — two indents
still pending when the innermost list composes its body:

> > - The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum
> >   of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
> > - A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote **inside** a list item is *legitimately* indented past
its item's text column by its own renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

- A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own before it that is long enough
  to wrap at the widths under test:

  > Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at every width under test, and
  > deliberately indented deeper than the item's own text column by the blockquote
  > renderer rather than by any defect.

  Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough to wrap, which must land
  back at the item's own text column rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows, exactly as fenced code
does everywhere else in this tool, and stays inside a recorded code range:

> A quote that introduces a command.
>
> ```bash
> some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
> ```
>
> Trailing prose after the fence.

A **one-line** fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that decides how strict the
sentinel walk has to be, because its whole content sits on a line that both opens and
closes the sentinel pair:

> ```
> one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim
> ```

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both passes that walk a composed
body meet a sentinel in the same document:

> - An item introducing a command:
>
>   ```sh
>   another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
>   ```

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool
carries at least four columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four
more on top of whatever its children already had — so a marker
glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is the
defect, not a style question.

        • A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has
          to wrap at least once at every width under test so that
          its continuation lines are visible next to its own marker
          rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
        • A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a
          continuation line, so that the alignment of the two items
          against each other can be compared directly at a width
          where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are
never substituted for a glyph, so the library still spells them as
digits when the last pass over the body runs:

        1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap
           so that the column its continuation lands at can be
           compared against the column its own text starts at.
        2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list
           under it so that the drift the re-alignment pass
           subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside
           one.
            ◦ A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap
              at the widths under test, so its own continuation
              column is observable.
            ◦ A second nested item, kept short.
        3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is
           still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted
prose under it does, and is reflowed through the same seam:

    ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to
    be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one
    line
    
    The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the
    two are checked against the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom
of it — two indents still pending when the innermost list composes
its body:

            • The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every
              width under test so that the sum of both quotes'
              indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
            • A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote inside a list item is
legitimately indented past its item's text column by its own
renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

    • A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own
      before it that is long enough to wrap at the widths under
      test:
          Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at
          every width under test, and deliberately indented deeper
          than the item's own text column by the blockquote
          renderer rather than by any defect.
      Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough
      to wrap, which must land back at the item's own text column
      rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows,
exactly as fenced code does everywhere else in this tool, and stays
inside a recorded code range:

    A quote that introduces a command.
    
        some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
    
    Trailing prose after the fence.

A one-line fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that
decides how strict the sentinel walk has to be, because its whole
content sits on a line that both opens and closes the sentinel
pair:

        one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both
passes that walk a composed body meet a sentinel in the same
document:

        • An item introducing a command:
              another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
        • A second item, long enough to wrap so that the item after
          a fence is still measured.

Plain quoted prose with no list in it at all, as the control: it is
reflowed by the library at the blockquote's own budget, so none of
its lines should need the safety net, and none of them should start
at column 0.

    A plain blockquoted paragraph with no list in it, long enough
    to wrap at every width under test, included because the same
    indent that the list case loses is the one this case loses too
    — the mechanism is the blockquote's, not the list's.

# Nested list continuation alignment

Fixture for WP-2e. Every item below is authored on a single source line, so nothing
here depends on the WP-2b loose path or the WP-2c tight-item coalescing pass: the only
thing under test is where a *nested* item's continuation lines land.

The mechanism this fixture exists to catch is `marked-terminal`'s `bulletPointLines` /
`numberedLines` adding a marker's width to every line an inner list already rendered as
a continuation, while leaving that inner list's marker lines alone. So each item that
has to demonstrate it is authored long enough to wrap **at every width the suite tests,
346 included** — a continuation that does not exist cannot be misaligned, and a fixture
that fits on one line at the widest real terminal would silently stop testing anything
there.

- A first-level unordered item, written at enough length that it wraps at 80 and 100 columns and gives the level-two items below it a parent whose own continuation alignment is worth checking at the same time.
  - A second-level unordered item, and this one is authored deliberately long enough that it still wraps even at 346 columns, which is the widest of the three tiled terminal layouts this tool is measured against, because the defect it demonstrates only becomes visible once a line has actually been wrapped and the wrapped remainder has somewhere to drift to. One ancestor level means one marker width of drift.
    - A third-level unordered item, also authored past 346 columns for the same reason, and this one sits under two ancestor levels rather than one, so before the fix its continuation lines drifted twice as far from their own marker's text column as the second-level item's did. Both are wrong; the deeper one is more wrong, and a fix that only handles one nesting level would pass a shallower fixture.
  - A second second-level item, short.
- A first-level item whose nested list is ordered, so the marker width the parent level adds is three columns rather than two:
  1. An ordered second-level item, authored long enough to wrap at 346 columns as well, because an ordered parent pads its non-marker lines with the width of a number and a full stop and a space rather than the two columns an unordered bullet costs, and a fix that hardcodes two would leave exactly one column of drift here and nowhere else.
     1. A third-level ordered item under an ordered parent, also past 346 columns, which is the case where two different marker widths compose and the drift is the sum of them rather than a multiple of either.
  2. A second ordered item, short.

1. A first-level *ordered* item, with an unordered sub-list, checking the mirror of the case above.
   - A second-level unordered item under an ordered parent, authored past 346 columns once more so that its continuation lines exist at every width under test and can be compared against the column its own bullet starts its text at.
   - A short sibling.
2. A second first-level ordered item, short.

- A first-level item whose nested item carries a fenced block, which is never rewritten:
  - A second-level item long enough to wrap at 346 columns, introducing a fence whose contents include lines that look like list markers, so that a re-alignment pass which is not sentinel-aware corrupts them visibly rather than subtly.

        echo "these four leading spaces are content, not indentation"

here depends on the WP-2b loose path or the WP-2c tight-item coalescing pass: the only
thing under test is where a *nested* item's continuation lines land.

The mechanism this fixture exists to catch is `marked-terminal`'s `bulletPointLines` /
`numberedLines` adding a marker's width to every line an inner list already rendered as
a continuation, while leaving that inner list's marker lines alone. So each item that
has to demonstrate it is authored long enough to wrap **at every width the suite tests,
346 included** — a continuation that does not exist cannot be misaligned, and a fixture
that fits on one line at the widest real terminal would silently stop testing anything
there.

- A first-level unordered item, written at enough length that it wraps at 80 and 100 columns and gives the level-two items below it a parent whose own continuation alignment is worth checking at the same time.
  - A second-level unordered item, and this one is authored deliberately long enough that it still wraps even at 346 columns, which is the widest of the three tiled terminal layouts this tool is measured against, because the defect it demonstrates only becomes visible once a line has actually been wrapped and the wrapped remainder has somewhere to drift to. One ancestor level means one marker width of drift.
    - A third-level unordered item, also authored past 346 columns for the same reason, and this one sits under two ancestor levels rather than one, so before the fix its continuation lines drifted twice as far from their own marker's text column as the second-level item's did. Both are wrong; the deeper one is more wrong, and a fix that only handles one nesting level would pass a shallower fixture.
  - A second second-level item, short.
- A first-level item whose nested list is ordered, so the marker width the parent level adds is three columns rather than two:
  1. An ordered second-level item, authored long enough to wrap at 346 columns as well, because an ordered parent pads its non-marker lines with the width of a number and a full stop and a space rather than the two columns an unordered bullet costs, and a fix that hardcodes two would leave exactly one column of drift here and nowhere else.
     1. A third-level ordered item under an ordered parent, also past 346 columns, which is the case where two different marker widths compose and the drift is the sum of them rather than a multiple of either.
  2. A second ordered item, short.

1. A first-level *ordered* item, with an unordered sub-list, checking the mirror of the case above.
   - A second-level unordered item under an ordered parent, authored past 346 columns once more so that its continuation lines exist at every width under test and can be compared against the column its own bullet starts its text at.
   - A short sibling.
2. A second first-level ordered item, short.

- A first-level item whose nested item carries a fenced block, which is never rewritten:
  - A second-level item long enough to wrap at 346 columns, introducing a fence whose contents include lines that look like list markers, so that a re-alignment pass which is not sentinel-aware corrupts them visibly rather than subtly.

    ```bash
    # * not a bullet, and 1. not a marker
    bun run --cwd mdview sweep
        echo "these four leading spaces are content, not indentation"
    ```

- A first-level item ending in a long token: https://example.invalid/a/long/url/inside/a/list/item/ok
  - See https://example.invalid/a/second/deliberately/long/url/inside/a/nested/list/item/which/must/also/survive/verbatim/ok

# Loose list probe

A loose list is any list where at least one item ends with a blank line. The lexer stamps looseness onto the whole list,
so every item below routes through mdview's own paragraph override even though only the separation between them is
blank.

## Loose list — the defect case

    • This first item is deliberately long enough that it must wrap across several rendered lines at any reasonable
      terminal width, so that the double-reflow defect has room to show itself clearly in the output stream.
    • The second item exists purely so that the list contains a blank line between items, which is what makes marked
      stamp the entire list as loose and route every item through mdview's own paragraph override, a live seam.
    • A third long item, again written at sufficient length that the wrapping engine has to break it multiple times,
      which is precisely the condition under which the orphaned trailing word appears at the end of each wrapped
      segment.

## Loose list with a nested loose list

    • An outer item carrying enough text to wrap at every width under test, so that the outer nesting level exercises
      the same wrapping budget the flat case does before recursion is considered at all.
        ◦ A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap, which matters because the nested level is wrapped against
          a strictly smaller budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower pass that runs
          afterwards.
        ◦ A second nested item, present so the inner list also ends an item on a blank line and is therefore stamped
          loose in its own right rather than inheriting the outer list's state.
    • A closing outer item, long enough to wrap, confirming that the outer list resumes at the outer budget once the
      nested list has been rendered and folded back into the parent body.

## Loose list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive

    • A hard break follows this sentence.
      And this sentence must begin a new rendered line of its own, even though the line before it is far too short to
      have been broken by any wrapping engine, and even though this item is long enough to wrap several times
      afterwards.
    • A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it, written long enough that it wraps at every
      width under test so that the item is not trivially short.

## Loose ordered list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide

    1. The first ordered loose item, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, so a budget computed
       from a hardcoded two-column marker would shear the tail of every line it produces.
    2. Second.
    3. Third.
    4. Fourth.
    5. Fifth.
    6. Sixth.
    7. Seventh.
    8. Eighth.
    9. Ninth.
    10. The tenth ordered loose item, also long enough to wrap at every width under test — this is the item whose marker
        is four columns wide rather than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong.

## Tight list — the control, must not change

    • A tight list item written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, which is the point: tight items
      never reach the paragraph override at all, so this rendering is the reference the loose case should match.
    • A second tight item, also long enough to wrap across multiple lines, with no blank line separating it from its
      neighbour so the lexer leaves the whole list tight.
    • A third tight item, again long, closing the control list without introducing any blank line that would flip the
      list into the loose branch being fixed.

## Ordered tight list — a second control

    1. An ordered tight item long enough to wrap, verifying that the ordered marker path is unaffected by whatever the
       loose-list fix does to the unordered one.
    2. A second ordered item, also long enough to wrap over several lines at the widths under test.

## Plain prose — the non-list control

This paragraph is not part of any list and is deliberately long enough to be reflowed by the paragraph renderer at every
width under test, so that any change to non-list prose wrapping shows up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather
than hiding in a corpus.

    A blockquote, also long enough to wrap at every width under test, included because the blockquote renderer reads the
    same reflow flag the paragraph renderer does and must therefore be held as a control alongside it.

# Tight list probe A *tight* list is any list where no item ends with a blank line. The lexer never wraps a tight item in a paragraph token, so `marked-terminal` never reflows it and the author's own line breaks reach the renderer verbatim. Every list below is tight, and every item is authored wrapped — the way real plans and briefs in this corpus are written. ## Tight list authored at about 115 columns — the defect case - The meaningful granularity here is per-item and per-batch, which is also where it really matters: the longest workflows are loops over files, and each pass through one of them re-reads the state that the previous pass has already written out, so the cost is quadratic in the number of items rather than linear in the number. - A second item, also authored wrapped at roughly the same column, present so that the list contains rather more than one item and the coalescing pass has an item boundary that it is forbidden to join across, in both of the directions, which a single-item fixture could never have demonstrated at any width at all. - A third item, again authored wrapped, closing the list without any blank line that would have flipped the whole thing into the loose branch that WP-2b already closed and that this fixture must not exercise here. ## Tight list authored at about 122 columns — the defect at the user's most-used width - An item authored wrapped at about one hundred and twenty-two columns, which is what a document written for a middling terminal looks like, and which therefore shears its tail at the narrower widths under test but not at the wider ones, giving the orphan metric a case at 116 and 120 that the hundred-column section above cannot produce for arithmetic. - A second item at the same authored column, so that this section too has an item boundary the coalescing pass must not join across, and so that its own last line is not also the last line of the list, which the metric would then skip. ## Tight list authored at about 170 columns — the defect at the widest real terminal - An item authored wrapped at roughly one hundred and seventy columns, which is what a document written for the widest of the three tiled terminal layouts looks like, and which therefore only shears its tail when the target width is narrower than the column the author wrapped at, so it exercises the same defect at a width the shorter items cannot reach. ## Tight list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive - A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it, authored wrapped and long enough that the item is not trivially short at any width under test, so the break is the only thing that can have put the second part on its own line. - A backslash hard break ends this line\ and this text follows that one, likewise authored wrapped so the item spans several rendered lines. - A break tag ends this line.
And this text follows the tag, again authored wrapped, so the tag is the only reason for the break. ## Tight list with a long URL and a long path on their own authored lines - The reference for this behaviour is recorded at https://example.invalid/a/deliberately/long/url/that/must/never/be/split/or/joined/mid-token/ok and the local copy lives at /home/example/some/deliberately/long/filesystem/path/that/must/also/survive/a/join/verbatim.md so both tokens can be checked, by eye and by assertion, on either side of a coalescing pass. ## Tight list with a fenced block inside an item — the fence is never rewritten - An item whose text is authored wrapped across two lines before the fence, so the coalescing pass has something to do in the same item that also carries a fence it must not touch: ```bash # * not a bullet, and 1. not a marker bun run --cwd mdview sweep echo "two spaces above are not a break" ``` ## Tight list with a nested tight list — no joining across the boundary - An outer item authored wrapped across two lines, so the outer level has a soft break of its own to coalesce before the nested list is reached at all. - A nested item, also authored wrapped across two lines, which is wrapped against a strictly smaller budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower pass that runs afterwards. - A second nested item, authored wrapped, so the inner list has an item boundary of its own too. - A closing outer item, authored wrapped, confirming the outer level resumes after the nested list has been rendered and folded back into the parent body. ## Ordered tight list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide 1. The first ordered tight item, authored wrapped, so a budget computed from a hardcoded two-column marker would shear the tail off every line it produces at the widths under test. 2. Second. 3. Third. 4. Fourth. 5. Fifth. 6. Sixth. 7. Seventh. 8. Eighth. 9. Ninth. 10. The tenth ordered tight item, also authored wrapped — this is the item whose marker is four columns wide rather than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong. ## Tight task list — the task-state sentinel must survive coalescing - [x] A completed task, authored wrapped across two lines, so the coalescing pass runs over text that carries the task-state sentinel between its bracket and its state character. - [/] An in-progress task in one of Obsidian's custom states, likewise authored wrapped across two lines so both the GFM-recognized and the custom-state paths are exercised here. ## Plain prose — the non-list control, must not change This paragraph is not part of any list and is authored wrapped exactly the way the items above are, so that any coalescing pass which leaked out of the list path would change this text and show up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather than hiding somewhere in a corpus.

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool carries at least four
columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four more on top of whatever its children
already had — so a marker glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is
the defect, not a style question.

> - A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has to wrap at least once at
>   every width under test so that its continuation lines are visible next to its own
>   marker rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
> - A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a continuation line, so that the
>   alignment of the two items against each other can be compared directly at a width
>   where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are never substituted for a
glyph, so the library still spells them as digits when the last pass over the body runs:

> 1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its
>    continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.
> 2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list under it so that the drift the
>    re-alignment pass subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside one.
>    - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap at the widths under test, so its
>      own continuation column is observable.
>    - A second nested item, kept short.
> 3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted prose under it does, and
is reflowed through the same seam:

> ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one line
>
> The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the two are checked against
> the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom of it — two indents
still pending when the innermost list composes its body:

> > - The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum
> >   of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
> > - A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote **inside** a list item is *legitimately* indented past
its item's text column by its own renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

- A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own before it that is long enough
  to wrap at the widths under test:

  > Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at every width under test, and
  > deliberately indented deeper than the item's own text column by the blockquote
  > renderer rather than by any defect.

  Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough to wrap, which must land
  back at the item's own text column rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows, exactly as fenced code
does everywhere else in this tool, and stays inside a recorded code range:

> A quote that introduces a command.
>
> ```bash
> some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
> ```
>
> Trailing prose after the fence.

A **one-line** fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that decides how strict the
sentinel walk has to be, because its whole content sits on a line that both opens and
closes the sentinel pair:

> ```
> one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim
> ```

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both passes that walk a composed
body meet a sentinel in the same document:

> - An item introducing a command:
>
>   ```sh
>   another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
>   ```
>
> - A second item, long enough to wrap so that the item after a fence is still measured.

Plain quoted prose with no list in it at all, as the control: it is reflowed by the
library at the blockquote's own budget, so none of its lines should need the safety net,
and none of them should start at column 0.

> A plain blockquoted paragraph with no list in it, long enough to wrap at every width
> under test, included because the same indent that the list case loses is the one this
> case loses too — the mechanism is the blockquote's, not the list's.

# Loose list probe

A loose list is any list where at least one item ends with a blank line. The
lexer stamps looseness onto the whole list, so every item below routes through
mdview's own paragraph override even though only the separation between them is
blank.

## Loose list — the defect case

    - This first item is deliberately long enough that it must wrap across
      several rendered lines at any reasonable terminal width, so that the
      double-reflow defect has room to show itself clearly in the output stream.
    - The second item exists purely so that the list contains a blank line
      between items, which is what makes marked stamp the entire list as loose
      and route every item through mdview's own paragraph override, a live seam.
    - A third long item, again written at sufficient length that the wrapping
      engine has to break it multiple times, which is precisely the condition
      under which the orphaned trailing word appears at the end of each wrapped
      segment.

## Loose list with a nested loose list

    - An outer item carrying enough text to wrap at every width under test, so
      that the outer nesting level exercises the same wrapping budget the flat
      case does before recursion is considered at all.
        - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap, which matters
          because the nested level is wrapped against a strictly smaller
          budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower
          pass that runs afterwards.
        - A second nested item, present so the inner list also ends an item on
          a blank line and is therefore stamped loose in its own right rather
          than inheriting the outer list's state.
    - A closing outer item, long enough to wrap, confirming that the outer list
      resumes at the outer budget once the nested list has been rendered and
      folded back into the parent body.

## Loose list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive

    - A hard break follows this sentence.
      And this sentence must begin a new rendered line of its own, even though
      the line before it is far too short to have been broken by any wrapping
      engine, and even though this item is long enough to wrap several times
      afterwards.
    - A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it,
      written long enough that it wraps at every width under test so that the
      item is not trivially short.

## Loose ordered list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide

    1. The first ordered loose item, written long enough that it wraps at every
       width under test, so a budget computed from a hardcoded two-column marker
       would shear the tail of every line it produces.
    2. Second.
    3. Third.
    4. Fourth.
    5. Fifth.
    6. Sixth.
    7. Seventh.
    8. Eighth.
    9. Ninth.
    10. The tenth ordered loose item, also long enough to wrap at every width
        under test — this is the item whose marker is four columns wide rather
        than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong.

## Tight list — the control, must not change

    - A tight list item written long enough that it wraps at every width under
      test, which is the point: tight items never reach the paragraph override
      at all, so this rendering is the reference the loose case should match.
    - A second tight item, also long enough to wrap across multiple lines, with
      no blank line separating it from its neighbour so the lexer leaves the
      whole list tight.
    - A third tight item, again long, closing the control list without
      introducing any blank line that would flip the list into the loose branch
      being fixed.

## Ordered tight list — a second control

    1. An ordered tight item long enough to wrap, verifying that the ordered
       marker path is unaffected by whatever the loose-list fix does to the
       unordered one.
    2. A second ordered item, also long enough to wrap over several lines at the
       widths under test.

## Plain prose — the non-list control

This paragraph is not part of any list and is deliberately long enough to be
reflowed by the paragraph renderer at every width under test, so that any change
to non-list prose wrapping shows up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather
than hiding in a corpus.

    A blockquote, also long enough to wrap at every width under test, included
    because the blockquote renderer reads the same reflow flag the paragraph
    renderer does and must therefore be held as a control alongside it.

# Nested list continuation alignment

Fixture for WP-2e. Every item below is authored on a single source line, so nothing
here depends on the WP-2b loose path or the WP-2c tight-item coalescing pass: the only
thing under test is where a *nested* item's continuation lines land.

The mechanism this fixture exists to catch is `marked-terminal`'s `bulletPointLines` /
`numberedLines` adding a marker's width to every line an inner list already rendered as
a continuation, while leaving that inner list's marker lines alone. So each item that
has to demonstrate it is authored long enough to wrap **at every width the suite tests,
346 included** — a continuation that does not exist cannot be misaligned, and a fixture
that fits on one line at the widest real terminal would silently stop testing anything
there.

- A first-level unordered item, written at enough length that it wraps at 80 and 100 columns and gives the level-two items below it a parent whose own continuation alignment is worth checking at the same time.
  - A second-level unordered item, and this one is authored deliberately long enough that it still wraps even at 346 columns, which is the widest of the three tiled terminal layouts this tool is measured against, because the defect it demonstrates only becomes visible once a line has actually been wrapped and the wrapped remainder has somewhere to drift to. One ancestor level means one marker width of drift.
    - A third-level unordered item, also authored past 346 columns for the same reason, and this one sits under two ancestor levels rather than one, so before the fix its continuation lines drifted twice as far from their own marker's text column as the second-level item's did. Both are wrong; the deeper one is more wrong, and a fix that only handles one nesting level would pass a shallower fixture.

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool carries at least four
columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four more on top of whatever its children
already had — so a marker glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is
the defect, not a style question.

> - A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has to wrap at least once at
>   every width under test so that its continuation lines are visible next to its own
>   marker rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
> - A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a continuation line, so that the
>   alignment of the two items against each other can be compared directly at a width
>   where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are never substituted for a
glyph, so the library still spells them as digits when the last pass over the body runs:

> 1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its
>    continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.
> 2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list under it so that the drift the
>    re-alignment pass subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside one.
>    - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap at the widths under test, so its
>      own continuation column is observable.
>    - A second nested item, kept short.
> 3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted prose under it does, and
is reflowed through the same seam:

> ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one line
>
> The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the two are checked against
> the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom of it — two indents
still pending when the innermost list composes its body:

> > - The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum
> >   of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
> > - A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote **inside** a list item is *legitimately* indented past
its item's text column by its own renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

- A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own before it that is long enough
  to wrap at the widths under test:

  > Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at every width under test, and
  > deliberately indented deeper than the item's own text column by the blockquote
  > renderer rather than by any defect.

  Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough to wrap, which must land
  back at the item's own text column rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows, exactly as fenced code
does everywhere else in this tool, and stays inside a recorded code range:

> A quote that introduces a command.
>
> ```bash
> some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
> ```
>
> Trailing prose after the fence.

A **one-line** fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that decides how strict the
sentinel walk has to be, because its whole content sits on a line that both opens and
closes the sentinel pair:

> ```
> one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim
> ```

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both passes that walk a composed
body meet a sentinel in the same document:

> - An item introducing a command:
>
>   ```sh
>   another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
>   ```
>
> - A second item, long enough to wrap so that the item after a fence is still measured.

Plain quoted prose with no list in it at all, as the control: it is reflowed by the
library at the blockquote's own budget, so none of its lines should need the safety net,
and none of them should start at column 0.

> A plain blockquoted paragraph with no list in it, long enough to wrap at every width
> under test, included because the same indent that the list case loses is the one this
> case loses too — the mechanism is the blockquote's, not the list's.

# Loose list probe A loose list is any list where at least one item ends with a blank line. The lexer stamps looseness onto the whole list, so every item below routes through mdview's own paragraph override even though only the separation between them is blank. ## Loose list — the defect case - This first item is deliberately long enough that it must wrap across several rendered lines at any reasonable terminal width, so that the double-reflow defect has room to show itself clearly in the output stream. - The second item exists purely so that the list contains a blank line between items, which is what makes marked stamp the entire list as loose and route every item through mdview's own paragraph override, a live seam. - A third long item, again written at sufficient length that the wrapping engine has to break it multiple times, which is precisely the condition under which the orphaned trailing word appears at the end of each wrapped segment. ## Loose list with a nested loose list - An outer item carrying enough text to wrap at every width under test, so that the outer nesting level exercises the same wrapping budget the flat case does before recursion is considered at all. - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap, which matters because the nested level is wrapped against a strictly smaller budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower pass that runs afterwards. - A second nested item, present so the inner list also ends an item on a blank line and is therefore stamped loose in its own right rather than inheriting the outer list's state. - A closing outer item, long enough to wrap, confirming that the outer list resumes at the outer budget once the nested list has been rendered and folded back into the parent body. ## Loose list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive - A hard break follows this sentence.
And this sentence must begin a new rendered line of its own, even though the line before it is far too short to have been broken by any wrapping engine, and even though this item is long enough to wrap several times afterwards. - A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test so that the item is not trivially short. ## Loose ordered list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide 1. The first ordered loose item, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, so a budget computed from a hardcoded two-column marker would shear the tail of every line it produces. 2. Second. 3. Third. 4. Fourth. 5. Fifth. 6. Sixth. 7. Seventh. 8. Eighth. 9. Ninth. 10. The tenth ordered loose item, also long enough to wrap at every width under test — this is the item whose marker is four columns wide rather than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong. ## Tight list — the control, must not change - A tight list item written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, which is the point: tight items never reach the paragraph override at all, so this rendering is the reference the loose case should match. - A second tight item, also long enough to wrap across multiple lines, with no blank line separating it from its neighbour so the lexer leaves the whole list tight. - A third tight item, again long, closing the control list without introducing any blank line that would flip the list into the loose branch being fixed. ## Ordered tight list — a second control 1. An ordered tight item long enough to wrap, verifying that the ordered marker path is unaffected by whatever the loose-list fix does to the unordered one. 2. A second ordered item, also long enough to wrap over several lines at the widths under test. ## Plain prose — the non-list control This paragraph is not part of any list and is deliberately long enough to be reflowed by the paragraph renderer at every width under test, so that any change to non-list prose wrapping shows up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather than hiding in a corpus. > A blockquote, also long enough to wrap at every width under test, included because the blockquote renderer reads the same reflow flag the paragraph renderer does and must therefore be held as a control alongside it.

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool carries at least four
columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four more on top of whatever its children
already had — so a marker glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is
the defect, not a style question.

> - A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has to wrap at least once at
>   every width under test so that its continuation lines are visible next to its own
>   marker rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
> - A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a continuation line, so that the
>   alignment of the two items against each other can be compared directly at a width
>   where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are never substituted for a
glyph, so the library still spells them as digits when the last pass over the body runs:

> 1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its
>    continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.
> 2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list under it so that the drift the
>    re-alignment pass subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside one.
>    - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap at the widths under test, so its
>      own continuation column is observable.
>    - A second nested item, kept short.
> 3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted prose under it does, and
is reflowed through the same seam:

> ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one line
>
> The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the two are checked against
> the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom of it — two indents
still pending when the innermost list composes its body:

> > - The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum
> >   of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
> > - A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote **inside** a list item is *legitimately* indented past
its item's text column by its own renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

- A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own before it that is long enough
  to wrap at the widths under test:

  > Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at every width under test, and
  > deliberately indented deeper than the item's own text column by the blockquote
  > renderer rather than by any defect.

  Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough to wrap, which must land
  back at the item's own text column rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows, exactly as fenced code
does everywhere else in this tool, and stays inside a recorded code range:

> A quote that introduces a command.
>
> ```bash
> some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
> ```
>
> Trailing prose after the fence.

A **one-line** fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that decides how strict the
sentinel walk has to be, because its whole content sits on a line that both opens and
closes the sentinel pair:

> ```
> one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim
> ```

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both passes that walk a composed
body meet a sentinel in the same document:

> - An item introducing a command:
>
>   ```sh
>   another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
>   ```
>
> - A second item, long enough to wrap so that the item after a fence is still measured.

Plain quoted prose with no list in it at all, as the control: it is reflowed by the
library at the blockquote's own budget, so none of its lines should need the safety net,
and none of them should start at column 0.

> A plain blockquoted paragraph with no list in it, long enough to wrap at every width
> under test, included because the same indent that the list case loses is the one this
> case loses too — the mechanism is the blockquote's, not the list's.

# Loose list probe A loose list is any list where at least one item ends with a blank line. The lexer stamps looseness onto the whole list, so every item below routes through mdview's own paragraph override even though only the separation between them is blank. ## Loose list — the defect case - This first item is deliberately long enough that it must wrap across several rendered lines at any reasonable terminal width, so that the double-reflow defect has room to show itself clearly in the output stream. - The second item exists purely so that the list contains a blank line between items, which is what makes marked stamp the entire list as loose and route every item through mdview's own paragraph override, a live seam. - A third long item, again written at sufficient length that the wrapping engine has to break it multiple times, which is precisely the condition under which the orphaned trailing word appears at the end of each wrapped segment. ## Loose list with a nested loose list - An outer item carrying enough text to wrap at every width under test, so that the outer nesting level exercises the same wrapping budget the flat case does before recursion is considered at all. - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap, which matters because the nested level is wrapped against a strictly smaller budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower pass that runs afterwards. - A second nested item, present so the inner list also ends an item on a blank line and is therefore stamped loose in its own right rather than inheriting the outer list's state. - A closing outer item, long enough to wrap, confirming that the outer list resumes at the outer budget once the nested list has been rendered and folded back into the parent body. ## Loose list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive - A hard break follows this sentence.
And this sentence must begin a new rendered line of its own, even though the line before it is far too short to have been broken by any wrapping engine, and even though this item is long enough to wrap several times afterwards. - A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test so that the item is not trivially short. ## Loose ordered list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide 1. The first ordered loose item, written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, so a budget computed from a hardcoded two-column marker would shear the tail of every line it produces. 2. Second. 3. Third. 4. Fourth. 5. Fifth. 6. Sixth. 7. Seventh. 8. Eighth. 9. Ninth. 10. The tenth ordered loose item, also long enough to wrap at every width under test — this is the item whose marker is four columns wide rather than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong. ## Tight list — the control, must not change - A tight list item written long enough that it wraps at every width under test, which is the point: tight items never reach the paragraph override at all, so this rendering is the reference the loose case should match. - A second tight item, also long enough to wrap across multiple lines, with no blank line separating it from its neighbour so the lexer leaves the whole list tight. - A third tight item, again long, closing the control list without introducing any blank line that would flip the list into the loose branch being fixed. ## Ordered tight list — a second control 1. An ordered tight item long enough to wrap, verifying that the ordered marker path is unaffected by whatever the loose-list fix does to the unordered one. 2. A second ordered item, also long enough to wrap over several lines at the widths under test. ## Plain prose — the non-list control This paragraph is not part of any list and is deliberately long enough to be reflowed by the paragraph renderer at every width under test, so that any change to non-list prose wrapping shows up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather than hiding in a corpus. > A blockquote, also long enough to wrap at every width under test, included because the blockquote renderer reads the same reflow flag the paragraph renderer does and must therefore be held as a control alongside it.

# Tight list probe A *tight* list is any list where no item ends with a blank line. The lexer never wraps a tight item in a paragraph token, so `marked-terminal` never reflows it and the author's own line breaks reach the renderer verbatim. Every list below is tight, and every item is authored wrapped — the way real plans and briefs in this corpus are written. ## Tight list authored at about 115 columns — the defect case - The meaningful granularity here is per-item and per-batch, which is also where it really matters: the longest workflows are loops over files, and each pass through one of them re-reads the state that the previous pass has already written out, so the cost is quadratic in the number of items rather than linear in the number. - A second item, also authored wrapped at roughly the same column, present so that the list contains rather more than one item and the coalescing pass has an item boundary that it is forbidden to join across, in both of the directions, which a single-item fixture could never have demonstrated at any width at all. - A third item, again authored wrapped, closing the list without any blank line that would have flipped the whole thing into the loose branch that WP-2b already closed and that this fixture must not exercise here. ## Tight list authored at about 122 columns — the defect at the user's most-used width - An item authored wrapped at about one hundred and twenty-two columns, which is what a document written for a middling terminal looks like, and which therefore shears its tail at the narrower widths under test but not at the wider ones, giving the orphan metric a case at 116 and 120 that the hundred-column section above cannot produce for arithmetic. - A second item at the same authored column, so that this section too has an item boundary the coalescing pass must not join across, and so that its own last line is not also the last line of the list, which the metric would then skip. ## Tight list authored at about 170 columns — the defect at the widest real terminal - An item authored wrapped at roughly one hundred and seventy columns, which is what a document written for the widest of the three tiled terminal layouts looks like, and which therefore only shears its tail when the target width is narrower than the column the author wrapped at, so it exercises the same defect at a width the shorter items cannot reach. ## Tight list with hard line breaks — the breaks must survive - A trailing double-space break ends this line, and this text follows it, authored wrapped and long enough that the item is not trivially short at any width under test, so the break is the only thing that can have put the second part on its own line. - A backslash hard break ends this line\ and this text follows that one, likewise authored wrapped so the item spans several rendered lines. - A break tag ends this line.
And this text follows the tag, again authored wrapped, so the tag is the only reason for the break. ## Tight list with a long URL and a long path on their own authored lines - The reference for this behaviour is recorded at https://example.invalid/a/deliberately/long/url/that/must/never/be/split/or/joined/mid-token/ok and the local copy lives at /home/example/some/deliberately/long/filesystem/path/that/must/also/survive/a/join/verbatim.md so both tokens can be checked, by eye and by assertion, on either side of a coalescing pass. ## Tight list with a fenced block inside an item — the fence is never rewritten - An item whose text is authored wrapped across two lines before the fence, so the coalescing pass has something to do in the same item that also carries a fence it must not touch: ```bash # * not a bullet, and 1. not a marker bun run --cwd mdview sweep echo "two spaces above are not a break" ``` ## Tight list with a nested tight list — no joining across the boundary - An outer item authored wrapped across two lines, so the outer level has a soft break of its own to coalesce before the nested list is reached at all. - A nested item, also authored wrapped across two lines, which is wrapped against a strictly smaller budget than its parent and must not be re-sheared by the shallower pass that runs afterwards. - A second nested item, authored wrapped, so the inner list has an item boundary of its own too. - A closing outer item, authored wrapped, confirming the outer level resumes after the nested list has been rendered and folded back into the parent body. ## Ordered tight list with ten items — the marker is four columns wide 1. The first ordered tight item, authored wrapped, so a budget computed from a hardcoded two-column marker would shear the tail off every line it produces at the widths under test. 2. Second. 3. Third. 4. Fourth. 5. Fifth. 6. Sixth. 7. Seventh. 8. Eighth. 9. Ninth. 10. The tenth ordered tight item, also authored wrapped — this is the item whose marker is four columns wide rather than three, and the one a hardcoded marker width gets wrong. ## Tight task list — the task-state sentinel must survive coalescing - [x] A completed task, authored wrapped across two lines, so the coalescing pass runs over text that carries the task-state sentinel between its bracket and its state character. - [/] An in-progress task in one of Obsidian's custom states, likewise authored wrapped across two lines so both the GFM-recognized and the custom-state paths are exercised here. ## Plain prose — the non-list control, must not change This paragraph is not part of any list and is authored wrapped exactly the way the items above are, so that any coalescing pass which leaked out of the list path would change this text and show up immediately as a diff in this fixture rather than hiding somewhere in a corpus.

# Lists inside blockquotes

The construct WP-2g exists for. Every list rendered by this tool carries at least four
columns of indent, and a blockquote adds four more on top of whatever its children
already had — so a marker glyph at column 0 anywhere in this file's rendered output is
the defect, not a style question.

> - A list item inside a blockquote, long enough that it has to wrap at least once at
>   every width under test so that its continuation lines are visible next to its own
>   marker rather than somewhere to the left of the quote.
> - A second item, also long enough to wrap onto a continuation line, so that the
>   alignment of the two items against each other can be compared directly at a width
>   where nothing has to wrap at all.

An ordered list, whose markers are wider than a bullet's and are never substituted for a
glyph, so the library still spells them as digits when the last pass over the body runs:

> 1. An ordered item inside a blockquote, long enough to wrap so that the column its
>    continuation lands at can be compared against the column its own text starts at.
> 2. A second ordered item, with a nested unordered list under it so that the drift the
>    re-alignment pass subtracts is exercised inside a quote as well as outside one.
>    - A nested item that is itself long enough to wrap at the widths under test, so its
>      own continuation column is observable.
>    - A second nested item, kept short.
> 3. A third ordered item, so the level's widest marker is still one character wide.

A heading inside a blockquote owes the same columns the quoted prose under it does, and
is reflowed through the same seam:

> ### A quoted heading, deliberately long enough that it has to be reflowed at the widths under test rather than fitting on one line
>
> The prose under that heading, also long enough to wrap, so the two are checked against
> the same budget.

A blockquote nested inside a blockquote, with a list at the bottom of it — two indents
still pending when the innermost list composes its body:

> > - The innermost item, long enough to wrap at every width under test so that the sum
> >   of both quotes' indents shows up in where its continuation lands.
> > - A second innermost item for comparison.

The other direction: a blockquote **inside** a list item is *legitimately* indented past
its item's text column by its own renderer, and nothing here may flatten it back.

- A list item that contains a quote, with prose of its own before it that is long enough
  to wrap at the widths under test:

  > Quoted prose inside a list item, long enough to wrap at every width under test, and
  > deliberately indented deeper than the item's own text column by the blockquote
  > renderer rather than by any defect.

  Trailing prose belonging to the same item, also long enough to wrap, which must land
  back at the item's own text column rather than at the quote's.

Fenced code inside a blockquote is never rewritten — it overflows, exactly as fenced code
does everywhere else in this tool, and stays inside a recorded code range:

> A quote that introduces a command.
>
> ```bash
> some-command --with a-very-long-argument --and another-long-one --so that this line is far past eighty columns
> ```
>
> Trailing prose after the fence.

A **one-line** fenced block inside a blockquote — the shape that decides how strict the
sentinel walk has to be, because its whole content sits on a line that both opens and
closes the sentinel pair:

> ```
> one-line fenced content that is comfortably longer than the narrowest width under test and must survive verbatim
> ```

A list inside a blockquote whose items carry a fence, so both passes that walk a composed
body meet a sentinel in the same document:

> - An item introducing a command:
>
>   ```sh
>   another-command --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value --flag value
>   ```
>
> - A second item, long enough to wrap so that the item after a fence is still measured.

Plain quoted prose with no list in it at all, as the control: it is reflowed by the
library at the blockquote's own budget, so none of its lines should need the safety net,
and none of them should start at column 0.

> A plain blockquoted paragraph with no list in it, long enough to wrap at every width
> under test, included because the same indent that the list case loses is the one this
> case loses too — the mechanism is the blockquote's, not the list's.

The WP-2f fixture. Two invariants live here, both invisible to every width gate:
`rewrapListBody` must never rewrite a line that belongs to a fenced block, and it must
never choose a line break that leaves a continuation line starting `*` or `N.`.

- A loose item whose fence carries a command far longer than any target width under
  test, which this pass used to split mid-command:

  ```bash
  echo "a deliberately very long command line that must never be rewrapped or reindented at all, at any width"
  ```

  walk has to be, because the block's opening and closing markers land on the same
  physical line and so that line never *starts* inside a fence:

  ```bash
  printf '%s\n' "one physical line, opening and closing marker both on it, and still far too long to fit"
  ```

- A tight item with a fence, whose content carries both marker shapes as decoys:
  ```text
  * not a bullet, and 1. not a marker, on a line long enough that the pass would have split it
  ```

- An outer item, long enough to wrap on its own, so that the level below it is not the
  only thing this pass has to look at.

  - A nested item whose fence has to survive the shallower level's pass as well as its
    own, since every level runs this pass over the body it just composed:

    ```bash
    git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all --since="2026-01-01" --author="nobody" | head -40
    ```

An ordered list, so the renumbering pass runs over a body that contains a fence:
